tw-mi-port-sheldon-capitalist-money.t: By 1913 one red building, then a barn, alone remained, and 'the lighthouse and harbor bell are now buried under the shifting sand dunes': the 1830s lighthouse site at the Pigeon Lake entrance lies under the dunes, a sign of how deep the drift is over the townsite. No digs reported.
src: Grand Rapids Press, 29 Dec 1921, p. 6, 'A Forgotten City by the Lake' No. IV, R. C. Meima (Newspapers.com 1111544215; same author as the Michigan History piece)

pinev: 1873 plat: N. A. Burton 160 = NW¼ sec 27 T2S R7W; Newbre farms across the S-line road; letter's paces put the well within ~120 m of the W quarter corner beside the 27/28 road.
W quarter corner from BLM PLSS (42.26852,-85.12030); the 27/28 road still shows on 2017 Michigan 1 m lidar; dry farmland.

The 1873 plat shows the graveyard at the SW corner of sec 27, matching the letter's graveyard reference; the well lies between it and the W quarter corner along the 27/28 road, nearer the quarter corner by the paces.

Free Press 15 Sep 1874: the well was about 5 mi SE of Battle Creek and about a mile from the Kalamazoo River, in N. A. Burton's pasture lot; the reporter paced from 'the half-mile stake' and found the distances exactly as the letter gave, which fits the W quarter corner of sec 27.

tw-mi-emmett-mcardill-dry-well-1874.st: The Free Press of 15 Sep 1874 adds that the well had been filled 12-14 years earlier and cropped over, and that the diggers were McArdill and his son, the well-digger Joe Jackson and three labourers.

tw-mi-cambridge-jct-walker-tavern-money-.t: The earliest period telling (Lansing State Journal, 1922) has only a 'gold laden traveler' murdered at the 1832 tavern and a bloodstain shown in the 'murder room' on tours; the buried money belt and the oak first appear in the 1941 WPA guide.
